title: Moody's Mark Zandi Says Tariffs Have Done Significant Damage to the Economy
description_short: Moody's chief economist Mark Zandi said in a May 2026 note that tariffs had done significant damage to the economy.
description_medium: Fortune reported on May 6, 2026, that Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi wrote in a note that tariff data were “definitive” and tariffs had “done significant damage to the economy.” CNBC's February report separately quoted Zandi warning that trade-policy uncertainty could restrain investment and hiring. These sources document his assessment, not the packet's separate household-cost estimate.
description_long: On May 6, 2026, Fortune reported that Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi wrote in a note that the data were “definitive” and that tariffs had “done significant damage to the economy.” Fortune's report attributes that conclusion to Zandi and describes it as his assessment of tariff effects. A February 23 CNBC report separately quoted Zandi saying uncertainty after the Supreme Court's tariff ruling could make businesses invest and hire less, while the article also described the unsettled tariff outlook. Together, these sources support an attributed account of Zandi's economic warning and the uncertainty he discussed. They do not establish a quantified causal estimate for household costs. The supplied CNBC link does not support the packet's additional May household-cost figures or its reference to costs from the U.S.-Iran war; those details are excluded. The title is revised from “confirms” to “says” so an economist's reported judgment is not presented as an independently proven statistical finding. This description reflects the source dates and claims available in the cited coverage.
notes: The populated medium attributes a May 6, 2026, statement to Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi and cites a May congressional study. The only linked CNBC URL is dated February 23, 2026, and covers the Supreme Court’s tariff ruling and Zandi’s comments about uncertainty; it cannot substantiate a later May statement or the household-cost figures. The packet provides no source for the May note or study.

The linked CNBC report is dated February 23, 2026 and covers the Supreme Court tariff ruling, new Section 122 tariffs, and Mark Zandi’s warning about economic uncertainty. It does not substantiate the supplied May 6 statement or the separate household-cost estimate. Add the Moody’s note and the cited study before combining those claims.

Wave3 evidence resolution (2026-10-03): Fortune reports that Zandi made the significant-damage statement in a note on May 6, 2026. CNBC's February 23 report separately quotes Zandi on uncertainty's potential effects on investment and hiring. Limitations: These sources report an economist's assessment; they do not provide a standalone causal estimate of tariff effects. The cited CNBC page does not support the separate $2,512 household cost, $1,745 comparison, or Iran-war cost claims in the prior description.
proposed_correction: Preserve the existing medium, but source the May 6 Zandi statement and Congressional study separately or revise the date and claims to match the linked February CNBC report.

title: Trump Called Jeffrey Epstein a “Terrific Guy” in a 2002 Interview
description_short: Trump's 2002 description of Epstein and later-reported social contact support an association, not claims of involvement in Epstein's crimes.
description_medium: A 2002 New York Magazine interview quoted Donald Trump saying he had known Jeffrey Epstein for 15 years and calling him a “terrific guy.” The New York Times later reported that Trump and Epstein attended a 1992 Mar-a-Lago party together, based on the event organizer's account; NBC News also described archived footage of them socializing. These sources document an association and public remarks, not involvement in Epstein's crimes.
description_long: A 2002 New York Magazine profile quoted Donald Trump saying, “I've known Jeff for fifteen years. Terrific guy,” and describing Epstein as someone who enjoyed socializing with women, including “many of them on the younger side.” The New York Times later reported that Trump and Jeffrey Epstein attended a 1992 party at Mar-a-Lago, citing the organizer's recollection that the two men were the only male guests among women invited to the event. NBC News separately described archived footage from the party showing the men together. These accounts support a narrower record of Trump's public praise and social association with Epstein. They do not establish that Trump took part in Epstein's criminal conduct, witnessed abuse, or knew of crimes. The existing linked New York Times article about Trump's 2024 criminal conviction does not support this relationship claim, so the proposed description adds the reporting that does. It keeps the event and quotation attributed to the sources and excludes the prior description's unsupported allegation that Trump was present at abuse of minors. An association or complimentary quote should not be treated as proof of criminal involvement.

title: Imaad Zuberi's Company Gave $900,000 to Trump's Inaugural Committee
description_short: Avenue Ventures, a company associated with donor Imaad Zuberi, gave $900,000 to Trump's 2017 inaugural committee; the sources do not show Qatar funded it.
description_medium: The New York Times reported that Avenue Ventures, Imaad Zuberi's California firm, gave $900,000 to Trump's inaugural committee after the 2016 election; a separate $100,000 went to the 2016 Republican convention fund. The report described a federal subpoena seeking inaugural-finance records, not a finding that Qatar's government made the contribution or that the Foreign Emoluments Clause was violated. The proposed title removes both unsupported assertions.
description_long: The New York Times reported that Imaad Zuberi's California firm, Avenue Ventures, paid $900,000 to Donald Trump's inaugural committee after the 2016 election. It separately reported a $100,000 contribution to help cover expenses of the 2016 Republican National Convention. Zuberi had met Qatari officials and accompanied a delegation to Trump Tower, but that contact does not show that Qatar's government supplied the inaugural contribution. The article describes federal prosecutors subpoenaing the inaugural committee for financial and event records as part of an inquiry; it does not report a finding that a foreign government made this payment or that the Foreign Emoluments Clause was violated. Associated Press coverage likewise identifies Avenue Ventures as the $900,000 donor and says the subpoena sought information about Zuberi and the committee. The corrected title identifies the documented contributor and amount. It drops the original claim of a $1 million foreign-government payment and the legal conclusion because neither is established by the linked report. The source supports a donation and an investigation, not a proven violation or a government-to-fund transfer.

title: Trump's EO 14215 Required White House Review of Independent Agencies' Significant Regulations
description_short: EO 14215 brought significant regulations from independent agencies into White House review; it did not make Trump the final arbiter of every prosecution.
description_medium: Executive Order 14215, signed February 18, 2025, required executive departments and agencies, including independent agencies, to submit significant proposed and final regulations to OIRA for White House review before publication. It also directed regular consultation with the White House and gave OMB roles in performance standards and agency apportionments. The order concerns regulatory oversight, not a general command over every prosecution or enforcement action.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14215, “Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies,” on February 18, 2025. The order states a policy of presidential supervision across the executive branch and requires executive departments and agencies, including independent agencies, to send significant proposed and final regulatory actions to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs for review before publication. It also directs regular consultation between independent-agency leaders and White House officials. The order gives the Office of Management and Budget roles in setting performance standards and reviewing independent agencies' spending apportionments, subject to applicable law. These provisions support a specific description of expanded presidential and White House oversight of regulatory agencies. The supplied Reuters link concerned control of independent agencies but did not support the record's broader statement that Trump became the final arbiter of every federal prosecution or regulatory action. The order text does not itself establish that all enforcement decisions were personally directed by Trump or that courts blocked the order. This revised account confines the claim to its documented review, consultation, and management provisions and does not infer a completed transfer of all law-enforcement authority.
notes:
The linked Reuters article returned 401 and concerns presidential control of independent agencies, not the executive order described in the synopsis. The packet provides no order text or matching court decisions; it does not identify which prosecutions or regulatory actions the order directed or halted.
Wave3 evidence resolution (2026-10-03): EO 14215 was signed February 18, 2025 and requires review of significant regulatory actions by OIRA before publication. The order provides for consultation with independent-agency chairs and OMB performance and apportionment roles, subject to law. Limitations: The order text supports regulatory and management oversight, not the claim that Trump personally became the final arbiter of every prosecution. The supplied packet includes no matching court decisions establishing that judges blocked the order.
proposed_correction: Identify the specific executive order and attach its text and the cited court decisions before describing it as making Trump the final arbiter of federal enforcement priorities.

title: Chicago Prosecutors Subpoenaed a Democratic Firm Tied to Judge Merchan's Daughter
description_short: A 2025 subpoena sought records from Authentic Campaigns, where Loren Merchan had been a vice president; motive claims remain commentary, not findings.
description_medium: A Boston Globe republication of New York Times reporting says Chicago prosecutors subpoenaed Authentic Campaigns in August 2025 for communications with Democratic clients. Loren Merchan, daughter of Judge Juan Merchan, had been a vice president of the firm until late 2024. Prosecutors later narrowed the request to a $468 Harris campaign payment and emails between Loren and her father. The reporting documents an inquiry, not a finding of political retaliation.
description_long: New York Times reporting carried by The Boston Globe says the U.S. attorney's office in Chicago investigated Authentic Campaigns, a Democratic fundraising firm once co-owned by Loren Merchan, daughter of New York Judge Juan Merchan. In August 2025, prosecutors subpoenaed the firm for a broad set of internal communications with clients, including Democratic political figures and organizations. The report says prosecutors later narrowed the request to a $468 payment from Kamala Harris's campaign and emails between Loren Merchan and her father. It identifies Matthew Skiba and William Hogan as the career prosecutors who secured the subpoena and notes their roles in the separate Broadview Six case. The original Emptywheel post interprets the inquiry as political retaliation, but the cited reporting does not establish that motive as an official finding. This narrower description records the subpoena, the firm's connection to the judge's daughter, and the reported narrowed scope. It does not state that the investigation proved wrongdoing by the firm, the judge, or the prosecutors, and it distinguishes the commentator's political interpretation from reported procedural facts.
notes: The linked Emptywheel post is commentary and makes the retaliation claim as an interpretation. It identifies a subpoena and the Broadview Six case but the supplied packet does not name the consulting firm, provide the subpoena or responses from the prosecutors, or establish a connection to Merchan's family. Those records are needed to verify the allegation.

The linked Emptywheel post is commentary and makes the retaliation claim as an interpretation. It identifies a subpoena investigation and the Broadview Six case but the packet does not name the consulting firm, reproduce the subpoena, include prosecutor responses, or establish a connection to Merchan's family. Those records are needed to verify the allegation.

Wave3 evidence resolution (2026-10-03): The reporting says Chicago prosecutors subpoenaed Authentic Campaigns in August 2025 and later narrowed the demand to a $468 Harris-campaign payment and emails between Loren and Juan Merchan. It identifies Loren Merchan as a former vice president and Matthew Skiba and William Hogan as prosecutors who secured the subpoena. Limitations: The cited reporting does not establish retaliatory intent as an official finding or prove wrongdoing by the firm or the judge. Emptywheel's characterization is commentary; the proposed factual account attributes that interpretation rather than stating it as fact.

title: Trump Pardoned Aviem Sella on January 19, 2021
description_short: The Justice Department lists Aviem Sella among Trump's January 19, 2021 pardons for specified federal offenses related to espionage charges.
description_medium: The Justice Department's clemency list places Aviem Sella under January 19, 2021 and names two espionage-conspiracy counts and an offense involving classified information received by a foreign agent. The archived White House says Trump granted Sella a full pardon and describes his 1986 indictment in the Jonathan Pollard case. The sources establish the pardon and listed charges, not a conviction or sentence.
description_long: The Justice Department's official clemency list places Aviem Sella in its January 19, 2021 section and lists the District of Columbia, no sentence, and offenses involving two counts of conspiracy to gather or deliver national-defense information and receiving or obtaining classified information as a foreign agent. The pardon instrument names Sella among those granted a full and unconditional pardon for the offenses enumerated for consideration. The archived White House's January 2021 statement says Trump granted Sella a full pardon and describes him as an Israeli citizen indicted in 1986 in connection with the Jonathan Pollard espionage case. Associated Press reporting says Sella was charged in absentia and was not extradited to the United States. These sources support the pardon date and the government's description of the charges. They do not establish that Sella was convicted, received a sentence, or that the pardon itself proves guilt or innocence. The input record's May 24, 2018 date conflicts with the official clemency list; this proposal uses the documented 2021 pardon date in the description and leaves the source metadata date for correction through the appropriate record process.
notes:
The linked DOJ pardon list places Sella in the January 19, 2021 group, conflicting with the input date May 24, 2018. It lists espionage-related offenses and no sentence but does not establish the case disposition or conduct. Proposed correction: verify the event date against the pardon instrument; do not silently replace the original date.
Wave3 evidence resolution (2026-10-03): The DOJ clemency list places Sella under January 19, 2021, lists specified espionage-related offenses, and gives no sentence. The archived White House statement says Trump granted Sella a full pardon and connects the 1986 indictment to the Jonathan Pollard case. AP reports Sella was charged in absentia and was not extradited to the United States. Limitations: The cited materials establish a pardon and list charges; they do not establish a conviction or sentence. The official pardon date conflicts with the entry's May 24, 2018 date, which should be corrected in source metadata separately.
